subject: history
subtitle: Elizabeth I's reign — religious settlement, the Spanish Armada, exploration, and the Golden Age.

data.targetWord: A person, usually Catholic, who refused to attend Church of England services and could be fined for this refusal.

examples.en-GB: Wealthy recusants sometimes paid their fines rather than change their Catholic beliefs.

data.targetWord: A small group of important advisers who helped the monarch govern England.

examples.en-GB: William Cecil was one of Elizabeth I's most trusted members of the Privy Council.

data.targetWord: A sailor who had government permission to attack enemy ships and take goods, effectively a state-sponsored pirate.

examples.en-GB: Francis Drake was a famous privateer who attacked Spanish treasure ships with Elizabeth I's approval.

data.targetWord: A large fleet of warships. The Spanish Armada was sent by Philip II of Spain in 1588 to invade England.

examples.en-GB: The Spanish Armada failed to invade England because of English tactics and severe storms.

data.targetWord: A ship deliberately set on fire and sent towards enemy vessels to cause panic and scatter their formation.

examples.en-GB: English fireships at Calais caused the Spanish fleet to scatter, disrupting their plan.

data.targetWord: The act of officially excluding someone from the Catholic Church. Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth I in 1570.

examples.en-GB: After excommunication in 1570, Catholics in England were formally released from obedience to Elizabeth.

data.targetWord: Elizabeth I's Catholic cousin who had a claim to the English throne and became the centre of plots against Elizabeth until her execution in 1587.

examples.en-GB: Mary Queen of Scots was kept under guard in England for nearly twenty years before her execution.

data.targetWord: A place settled and controlled by people from another country. Elizabethan England made early attempts to establish colonies in North America.

examples.en-GB: Roanoke was an early English colony attempt in North America that ultimately failed.

data.targetWord: A positive interpretation of Elizabeth I's reign that emphasises cultural achievement, the Armada victory, and national confidence, though historians debate whether it applied to all people.

examples.en-GB: The 'Golden Age' interpretation highlights Shakespeare, exploration, and the defeat of the Armada, but many people still faced poverty.

data.targetWord: A 1559 law requiring people to attend Church of England services and follow the official prayer book.

examples.en-GB: The Act of Uniformity meant that Catholics who stayed away from Church of England services could be fined.

data.targetWord: A 1586 Catholic plot involving letters that apparently showed Mary Queen of Scots agreeing to Elizabeth I's assassination.

examples.en-GB: Evidence uncovered in the Babington Plot led to the trial and execution of Mary Queen of Scots.

data.targetWord: A naval battle in July 1588 where English ships damaged the Spanish Armada and prevented it from linking with Parma's army in the Netherlands.

examples.en-GB: The Battle of Gravelines was a turning point that effectively ended Spain's hope of invading England.

data.targetWord: Elizabeth I's secretary and spymaster who built a network of spies to uncover Catholic plots against the queen.

examples.en-GB: Francis Walsingham uncovered the Babington Plot through his network of spies and informers.

data.targetWord: Elizabethan laws that organised poor relief through local parishes, collecting rates to support the deserving poor while punishing those considered idle.

examples.en-GB: The 1601 Poor Law made parishes responsible for collecting money to support aged and sick poor people.

data.targetWord: In Tudor law, a person without settled work or a fixed home who could be punished under poor law regulations.

examples.en-GB: Elizabethan poor laws treated vagabonds harshly, sometimes having them whipped and returned to their home parish.

data.targetWord: An Elizabethan naval commander and slave trader whose voyages in the 1560s represent the darker side of Elizabethan expansion.

examples.en-GB: John Hawkins was involved in slave trading voyages to West Africa and the Americas in the 1560s.

data.targetWord: Elizabeth I's trusted chief adviser and Lord Burghley, who helped shape English government and foreign policy for decades.

examples.en-GB: William Cecil served Elizabeth I for nearly forty years, helping to manage government and navigate threats.

data.targetWord: A 1569 uprising by Catholic nobles in northern England who hoped to restore Catholic influence and support Mary Queen of Scots.

examples.en-GB: The Northern Rebellion of 1569 showed that some English Catholics were willing to take up arms against Elizabeth I.

data.targetWord: A journey made by a Tudor monarch around the country, staying at noble houses, to show royal presence and win loyalty.

examples.en-GB: Elizabeth I used royal progresses to show herself to her subjects and reward loyal nobles.

data.targetWord: An Elizabethan courtier, explorer and promoter of colonisation who organised attempts to settle Roanoke in North America.

examples.en-GB: Walter Raleigh financed the Roanoke colony, one of England's first attempts to establish a permanent settlement in North America.

data.targetWord: A historian's view or explanation of the past, shaped by the questions they ask, the evidence they use, and their perspective.

examples.en-GB: Whether Elizabeth's reign was a 'Golden Age' depends on whose interpretation you accept and which evidence you emphasise.

data.targetWord: The Spanish military commander in the Netherlands whose army the Armada was meant to collect and escort to invade England.

examples.en-GB: The Armada's failure to link with the Duke of Parma's army was a key reason Spain could not invade England.

data.targetWord: Elizabethan term for people considered unable to work through age, sickness or disability, who were entitled to parish support.

examples.en-GB: The Elizabethan Poor Laws distinguished between the deserving poor and those seen as idle beggars.

data.targetWord: Information about a source's origin: who made it, when, why, and for whom, used to judge how useful it is as evidence.

examples.en-GB: The provenance of a royal portrait tells us it was designed to show power, not to record Elizabeth's real appearance.

data.targetWord: Catholic king of Spain who sent the Armada against England in 1588, motivated by religion, politics, and English interference in Spanish affairs.

examples.en-GB: Philip II of Spain organised the Armada partly to defend Catholicism and partly to stop English attacks on Spanish ships.

data.targetWord: A famous Elizabethan theatre in London associated with William Shakespeare's company, where plays were performed for audiences of different social classes.

examples.en-GB: The Globe Theatre could hold thousands of spectators who paid to watch Shakespeare's plays.

data.sentence: Elizabeth I became queen in ____ after the death of Mary I.
The Elizabethan Religious Settlement was introduced in ____, creating a Protestant Church with some traditional features.
Elizabeth I took the title 'Supreme ____' of the Church, not Supreme Head.
Pope Pius V ____ Elizabeth I in 1570, releasing Catholics from obedience to her.
Mary Queen of Scots fled to England in ____ and became Elizabeth's prisoner.
Mary Queen of Scots was executed in ____ after the Babington Plot.
The Spanish Armada was sent by ____ II of Spain in 1588.
The Spanish Armada anchored near ____ before the fireship attack scattered the fleet.
One major reason the Armada failed was its inability to link up with the Duke of ____'s army in the Netherlands.
Francis Drake's raid on Cadiz in 1587 is sometimes called 'singeing the King of Spain's ____'.
The 1601 ____ Law made parishes responsible for organising poor relief.
Elizabeth I's spymaster ____ uncovered many Catholic plots including the Babington Plot.
The English settlement attempt at ____ in North America ultimately failed.
John ____ was an Elizabethan sailor linked to the slave trade in the 1560s.
Elizabeth I's reign ended in ____ when she died and James VI of Scotland became James I of England.
The ____ were strict Protestants who wanted the Church of England to remove more Catholic-style practices.
Elizabeth's legitimacy was questioned by some Catholics because they rejected her mother ____ Boleyn's marriage to Henry VIII.
After its defeat, the Armada sailed north around ____ and Ireland, suffering terrible losses in storms.
William ____, Lord Burghley, was Elizabeth I's most trusted and long-serving adviser.
The ____ Plot of 1571 planned to replace Elizabeth with Mary Queen of Scots and involved foreign support.

pairs.text: Philip II wanted to defend Catholicism
England supported Protestant rebels in the Netherlands
Mary Queen of Scots was executed in 1587
English privateers attacked Spanish treasure ships
England competed with Spain for trade routes

Poverty increased due to poor harvests in the 1590s
Catholics and Puritans both faced punishment
